Side effects

Thymosin Alpha-1 side effects

In clinical studies of Thymosin Alpha-1, mostly at 1.6 mg under the skin, the most common side effects were irritation, redness or discomfort at the injection site.1 The most serious reports came from stem cell transplant recipients: engraftment failure and fatal immune destruction of red blood cells.12 FDA also warns of possible immune reactions to compounded Ta1.7

How often side effects were reported

The safety record of Thymosin Alpha-1 (Ta1) comes from clinical studies, mostly in patients with infections or cancer, who usually received 1.6 mg under the skin.12 In those studies, the most common side effects were local irritation, redness or discomfort at the injection site.1 In most studies, Ta1 was not linked to significant adverse events at doses of 1 to 16 mg under the skin for up to 12 months.1

Larger studies and label data point the same way:

  • TESTS sepsis trial (2025), 1,106 adults, double blind: no safety outcome differed significantly between Ta1 and placebo.3
  • Hepatitis B trial (1998), 98 patients, randomized: the authors observed no significant side effects.4
  • Flu vaccine trial (1989), 90 men aged 65 to 99, double blind: no toxicity was seen in either group.5
  • Metastatic melanoma trial (2010), 488 patients: adding Ta1 to dacarbazine and interferon alfa caused no extra toxicity.6
  • Zadaxin label, Indonesia (as summarized by FDA): drug-related adverse events occurred in under 1% of more than 2,000 people.2
  • Post-marketing estimate (2016 book chapter): authors working for or advising Zadaxin's maker reported over 17 million doses in an estimated 350,000 or more people, with infrequent, mild adverse experiences.2 This is an estimate linked to the manufacturer, not a controlled study.2

Reported side effects by frequency

Most common

  • Injection-site reactions: irritation, redness or discomfort where the injection was given, the complaint seen most across studies.1
  • Italy's Zadaxin label (as summarized by FDA) reports no clinically appreciable side effects apart from occasional modest, temporary pain at the injection site.2

Rare, per the Indonesian label

  • Redness of the skin (erythema), temporary muscle wasting (transient muscle atrophy), joint pain with hand swelling (polyarthralgia with hand edema) and rash.2

Reported in single studies or case reports

  • Liver enzyme flares: in chronic hepatitis B, the Indonesian label says ALT can rise temporarily to more than twice its starting level during treatment.2 It says treatment is generally continued unless signs of liver failure appear.21
  • Thyroid changes: TSH abnormalities were reported in a hepatitis C study.1 One FDA adverse event report described anxiety, atrial fibrillation and a temporary TSH drop in a man also taking peginterferon, so the cause is unclear.1
  • Fever and nausea: in a 1982 phase 1 study of 14 people with advanced cancer given single doses into the muscle, 1 had fever (at 2.4 mg/m2) and 2 had mild nausea (at 4.8 and 9.6 mg/m2).2
  • Nipple pain: reported in one liver cancer study of 25 patients.1

Serious events

  • Stem cell transplant recipients: graft failure (engraftment failure) and fatal immune hemolytic anemia, in which the immune system destroys red blood cells, were reported with Ta1.12
  • Infections after transplant: a case series in these patients found more infections with Ta1.1
  • FDA's reading: Ta1 could cause or worsen graft-versus-host disease and engraftment failure in stem cell transplant patients.21

Risks FDA flagged in 2024

  • Immune reactions: FDA says compounded Ta1 may pose a significant risk of immunogenicity, an immune response against the peptide, for certain routes of administration.7
  • Poor characterization: FDA found key data on impurities, aggregates and bacterial endotoxin missing for both the free base and the acetate.1 It called the substance sensitive to formulation, processing and environmental conditions that may lead to aggregation and degradation.1
  • Vaccines: FDA says safety data are too limited to judge the right dose or the risks of giving Ta1 with flu vaccines.1 It adds that putting an immune modulator into any vaccine could raise unknown safety concerns.1

Warnings on labels abroad

FDA's 2024 review summarizes these warnings from Zadaxin labels outside the US.2

  • Deliberate immune suppression: the Indonesian label says Zadaxin should be considered contraindicated in people kept immunosuppressed on purpose, such as organ transplant patients, unless benefits clearly outweigh risks.2
  • Children, pregnancy and breastfeeding: Italy's label says it should not be used in children and is contraindicated in pregnancy and breastfeeding.2
  • Autoimmune disease and allergy: Italy's label says use in autoimmune disease must be judged case by case, with caution in atopic people or anyone with past allergic reactions.21
  • Other immune medicines: Italy's label advises caution when Zadaxin is combined with other immunomodulatory drugs, because Ta1 acts on lymphocyte function.2

Animal safety data

According to the Zadaxin product monograph as summarized by FDA, single doses up to 20 mg/kg caused no drug-related safety signals in mice, rats and marmosets.1 Neither did repeated doses under the skin of up to 6 mg/kg a day for 13 weeks, or 1 mg/kg a day for 26 weeks.1 FDA could not review the underlying data, and it found no carcinogenicity studies and no published reproductive toxicity data.1 These are animal results and say nothing direct about people.

Research vials are a separate question

The human data on this page come from Zadaxin and from trial drug given under medical care.12 FDA notes that Zadaxin is a finished drug product that cannot be used interchangeably with Ta1 as a substance.2 Health Canada warns that unauthorized injectable peptides, thymosin alpha among them, may contain high-risk ingredients, additives or contaminants that may or may not be listed on the label.8 The vial sold on this site is labeled: For research use only. Not for human or veterinary use.

Frequently asked questions

What are the common side effects of thymosin alpha 1?

The most common in clinical studies were irritation, redness or discomfort at the injection site, and in most studies Ta1 was not linked to significant adverse events.1 The Indonesian label for the brand Zadaxin, as summarized by FDA, lists rare redness, temporary muscle wasting, joint pain with hand swelling, and rash.2 In an early cancer study, 1 of 14 people had fever and 2 had mild nausea after single doses into the muscle.2

Is thymosin alpha 1 safe?

In studies under medical care, mostly at 1.6 mg under the skin, it was generally well tolerated, and injection-site reactions were the main complaint.1 Still, FDA judged its safety information inadequate, warned of possible immune reactions to compounded Ta1, and noted serious harms in stem cell transplant recipients.71 Labels abroad advise against use in children, in pregnancy and breastfeeding, and in people kept immunosuppressed on purpose.2 Health Canada warns that unauthorized injectable peptides, thymosin alpha among them, may contain high-risk ingredients or contaminants that may or may not be listed on the label.8

Can thymosin alpha 1 cause an immune reaction?

FDA says compounded Ta1 may pose a significant risk of immunogenicity, meaning an immune response against the peptide itself, for certain routes of administration.7 Its review adds that clumping (aggregation) and peptide-related impurities could make this worse, and that a solution stronger than 2 mg/mL, the highest strength it found in clinical studies, could raise the risk.1 FDA listed the lack of information on immunogenicity among its reasons for calling the safety data insufficient.1

Is thymosin alpha 1 safe during pregnancy?

Italy's Zadaxin label, as summarized by FDA, says the medicine is contraindicated during pregnancy and breastfeeding and should not be used in children.2 FDA's 2024 review also found no published reproductive toxicity data for Ta1 and no carcinogenicity studies, and it could not check the animal safety data in the maker's monograph.1
